anomaly_def.Name: Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description: Definition: Root cause located at the storage capacity dimension, where the physical or logical free space allocated to data files, indexes, tablespaces, transaction logs, archive logs, rollback areas, temporary work areas, backup destinations, or diagnostic logs reaches a hard boundary. It is distinct from I/O throughput anomalies because the failure mode is space exhaustion rather than bandwidth or latency. Observable phenomena: rapidly declining free space, data-file or tablespace auto-extension failures, allocation-failed or no-space errors raised to clients and recorded in engine logs, log and archive destinations becoming full, temporary-space failures during sorts, hash operations, or index builds, backup-area saturation, and cascading stalls when log segments cannot be recycled or archives cannot be written. Possible contributing factors: uncontrolled data growth without retention or partition rotation, burst data-load or replication activity, oversized or orphaned temporary objects and large object payloads, missing log and archive cleanup policies, auto-extension disabled or capped below realistic peak demand, failed maintenance jobs that would normally reclaim space, backup retention silently retaining old sets, and monitoring tied only to percentage thresholds rather than to absolute free space and growth velocity.

entry.official_definition: Maximum amount of time allowed to complete client authentication; if not completed in time, the server closes the connection.
entry.trigger_condition: A would-be client does not complete the authentication protocol within authentication_timeout.
entry.workload_impact: The server closes the connection attempt, preventing hung clients from occupying a connection indefinitely.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
